The problem

A straight line on a map tells you almost nothing about whether a patient can actually reach a doctor.

Physical distance is a poor proxy for access. The same kilometre behaves differently depending on the road, the terrain, the traffic and the traveller. The project's founding question — “how long is a mile?” — reframes accessibility around travel time and real service availability rather than as-the-crow-flies proximity.

What bends a mile
Road quality · paved vs. track Terrain · hills & waterways Traffic & speed limits Transport mode · car · foot Public transit availability Socio-economic · age · disability Car ownership Provider capacity · physicians
Objective

Build a reproducible accessibility indicator that lets the Bank identify under-served populations, target investment where it closes the widest gaps, and measure the impact of new facilities — so that no one is left behind.

Theoretical foundations

Accessibility as the meeting point of supply and demand

Spatial accessibility is the ability to move from where people live to where a service is offered — an essential determinant of the relationship between supply (health professionals) and demand (population).

The gravity model

Borrowed from physics: the shorter the distance between two places — and the greater the “mass” of either — the stronger the pull between them. Applied to health, it models the flow between residential areas and the location of a service, weighted by a travel-friction coefficient.

This gravity family is the theoretical backbone of the project's accessibility scoring, and it distinguishes mere proximity from genuine, capacity-aware access.

Grounded in the literature

Luo, W. & Wang, F. (2003). Measures of Spatial Accessibility to Healthcare in a GIS Environment: Synthesis and a Case Study in the Chicago Region. Environ. Plann. B, 30(6): 865–884.

Method family
2SFCA · two-step 3SFCA · three-step M2SFCA · modified CB2SFCA · commuter-based
Two complementary approaches

Proximity is one question. Availability is another.

The project measures accessibility along two distinct axes. The first asks how far the nearest service is; the second asks whether that service is actually sufficient for everyone who depends on it.

Approach A

The Distance Approach

“How far — in time — is the nearest facility?”

  • matrix
    Distance Matrix

    Pairwise travel time & distance between every population point and its k nearest facilities.

  • O–D
    Origin–Destination Matrix

    Shortest paths computed over the real road network, origin to destination.

  • isochrone
    Isochrone Zones

    Areas reachable within a given time budget around each facility.

A supply-side, geographic measure of proximity. Fast to compute, but blind to how many people compete for the same doctor.
Approach B

The Gravity Model

“Given demand and friction, is the service enough?”

  • ratio
    Provider-to-population ratio

    Physicians divided by the population inside each facility's catchment.

  • 2SFCA
    Two-Step Floating Catchment Area

    The core method — sums competing catchments to score access per location.

  • friction
    Travel-friction weighting

    Distance decay applied so nearer services count for more than distant ones.

A supply-and-demand measure of availability. Captures competition and provider capacity that raw distance ignores.

The two are not rivals — they compose. The Distance Approach produces the travel times dij that are fed as the friction input into the Gravity Model. One says “how far”; the other says “with what real level of service.”

Methodology

From open data to an accessibility score

A four-stage pipeline turns raw geodata into a per-location indicator, combining people, providers and the road network that connects them.

Prepare the layers

Population and facility points cleaned, geo-referenced and reduced to centroids on a grid.

QGIS · OSM · Overpass

Build the matrix

Nearest-neighbour links each population point to its k = 3 closest facilities.

spatial index · N·k×3

Compute travel time

A local routing engine returns real driving times over the road graph.

OSRM · Docker · MLD

Score with 2SFCA

Two floating-catchment passes yield the accessibility index per residence.

Java · d₀ threshold
The 2SFCA algorithm

Two “floating catchments” sweep the map. The first sets each facility's supply ratio against the population it can serve; the second sums, for every residence, the ratios of all facilities within reach. A larger score means better access.

Where Pk is the population of tract k, Sj the physicians at facility j, and d the travel time within threshold d₀.

Step 1
Rj = Sj / Σ Pk

Facility supply ratio. For each facility j, gather all population k within travel time d₀ and divide its physicians by that catchment population.

Step 2
Ai = Σ Rj

Accessibility at a residence. For each location i, sum the supply ratios of every facility j reachable within d₀. Higher Ai = better access.

Data & architecture

Open data on an open, distributed stack

Every input is open; every component is open-source and built to be distributed, fault-tolerant, scalable and reproducible — country by country, provisioned entirely as code.

Use case — Kigali, Rwanda

The full pipeline, run end-to-end on one city

Kigali served as the proof of concept: roughly 1,239 villages, ~600 facilities and 1.7 million population points, taken from raw geodata all the way to an accessibility map and live dashboard.

Results

What the indicator revealed

Running 2SFCA over Kigali surfaced concrete, threshold-sensitive gaps — the kind of evidence that turns a map into an investment decision.

9.30%

of the population fall in poor accessibility (2SFCA ≤ 0.50) at a driving threshold of d₀ = 1,800 s — the baseline under-served share.

12–13%

under-served when the catchment tightens to d₀ = 900 s — a stricter time budget reveals more vulnerable residents.

63.21%

of population points lie within 2,500 m of a facility (k = 3) — most of the city is close, which is exactly why the gravity view matters for the rest.

82,085

routed records indexed, at an average distance of 13,093.9 m — the measured backbone behind every accessibility score.

Interpretation: the distance view says most of Kigali is near a clinic; the gravity view says a meaningful minority still lack sufficient access once provider capacity and competition are counted. That gap is the target.

Impact & roadmap

From one city to a continental indicator

EVIDENCE

Target investment

An objective, reproducible basis for placing new facilities where they close the widest access gaps — and for measuring impact afterward.

OPEN

Open & sovereign

Built entirely on open data and open technologies, keeping cost low and the method fully in the hands of national teams.

SCALE

Replicable by design

Infrastructure-as-code and per-country subnets mean the whole stack redeploys city by city, and extends to education and other public services.

Next: 14 countries

Kigali proved the method. The roadmap scales the healthcare accessibility indicator across fourteen African nations — and reframes the question from “where is the gap?” to “where should the next service go?”
